title: o11 vs. Composio vs. Arcade: Tool Execution, Accounts, and Authentication
summary: Compare tool execution and account authorization across o11, Composio, and Arcade, with a practical lifecycle pilot for agent developers.
body_markdown:
Choose between o11, Composio, and Arcade by identifying what currently prevents your agent from completing work. It might need access to a paid service, permission to act inside a customer’s account, or a reliable way to discover and execute tools. Those needs overlap, but they are not interchangeable.


For a developer, the practical goal is fewer pieces of integration work between an idea and a useful result. That includes credential setup, tool descriptions, user authorization, error handling, and the lifecycle of any paid job.


**Reviewed October 18, 2026. Disclosure:** this article is published by o11. Vendor descriptions were checked against official documentation. This is not a hands-on performance comparison, and we made no paid supplier calls. The o11 discussion reflects inspected local implementation and audit evidence; deployed supplier access was not inspected.


## Separate access from capability


Consider two requests: research a public company’s competitors, and read the latest messages in a customer’s private Slack channel. The first may require purchasing search and retrieval. The second requires authorization to the correct customer’s existing account. Paying for an API does not grant access to that private channel.


A third request, posting the resulting brief into Slack, adds a mutation. A tool can be discoverable without being authorized to perform that write. A model choosing the tool does not establish that the user approved the action.


The architecture needs clear answers at each boundary: which tool is appropriate; whose identity it uses; whether it can read or write; how any provider usage is funded; and what evidence establishes completion.


That is why comparing only the number of integrations produces weak decisions. A smaller set with the right identity and exact actions can be more useful than a much larger catalog that requires custom work for the operations you intend to ship. The[agent tool gateway guide](https://o11.ai/blog/what-is-an-ai-tool-gateway) explains the responsibilities a unified access layer can take on.


## What the three platforms emphasize


Composio’s current developer documentation presents managed authentication, sessions, tool discovery, and execution. It supports exposing a session through MCP as well as framework integrations. This makes it relevant when an agent works across multiple connected applications. Assess a concrete session and user, rather than treating a project API key as the end customer’s authorization.[Composio developer documentation](https://docs.composio.dev/docs) .


Arcade documents an authorization flow in which tool execution checks the user’s required permissions and can return a consent challenge. The tool runs with the resulting credential supplied through its execution context, without requiring the model to handle the provider token. That is directly relevant to user-authorized actions in existing services.[Arcade authorized tool calling](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/tool-calling/custom-apps/auth-tool-calling) .


o11’s inspected local implementation combines a capability catalog with customer accounts and wallet-funded operations. It exposes discovery, contract inspection, quoting, invocation, status, and cancellation through credentials bound to a spending card. The card carries the agent’s policy and allowance; credential rotation preserves that identity and history. The practical question is whether a required supplier operation is activated for your workspace, with the correct funding path and verified result. Implemented contracts and locally checked adapters are not live supplier certification.


## A task-oriented comparison


Your requirement Evidence to request Why it matters


Read a user’s existing business data Consent flow, identity binding, read scopes, refresh behavior A tool list does not establish access to the right tenant


Perform a business action Exact write scope, approval rule, execution receipt Read permission is not permission to send or publish


Purchase a new capability Supported funded operation, current price, enforced limit Connected-account support alone does not remove supplier signup


Run an unfamiliar tool Accurate schema, examples, typed errors Discovery must turn into correct execution


Operate unattended Revocation, job recovery, logs, ownership A successful demo does not cover a failed overnight run


Apply every row to all three platforms. Avoid scoring a product down because you have not found a public page for a requirement. Mark the item unverified, ask for evidence, and decide whether the uncertainty is acceptable for your launch.


This approach also prevents a common category mistake: assuming that a platform’s strong OAuth support necessarily includes subsidized or shared paid access to every provider, or that a paid catalog necessarily supports every account-owned business action.


## Paid tools and connected apps can coexist


Composio Instant adds supported paid actions to Composio’s connected-app model. Its current documentation describes provider-account execution charged to a Composio balance, alongside the ability to retain users’ own connections. Check which tool actions support Instant and whether your project has access. It is not accurate to characterize Composio as connected accounts only.[Composio Instant Tools](https://docs.composio.dev/docs/instant-tools) .


For Arcade, the documentation reviewed establishes authorization and tool execution. It does not by itself establish that an arbitrary paid API is included in a shared supplier balance. If that is your main requirement, request the exact supported commercial path instead of making an assumption in either direction.


For o11, customer-account calls in the inspected local implementation do not debit wallet credits; the provider relationship remains with that account. Wallet-funded operations require configured supplier credentials and usable pricing evidence. Card funding is disabled in the inspected local configuration; this is not a verification of a deployed service’s settings.


A mixed workflow can use connected Slack access and purchased web research without pretending that they have the same ownership model. The application should preserve that distinction in activity records. Read[customer accounts and pay-per-use tools](https://o11.ai/blog/provider-accounts-and-pay-per-use-tools) before setting automatic account precedence.


## Authorization is a product flow


An authorization challenge arrives at an inconvenient moment: the agent has already started a task. Your product must explain what is missing, let the user authorize the intended account, and resume useful work afterward. A raw provider error is rarely enough.


Evaluate first-time consent and reconnection separately. First-time access can require a user interaction. An expired token may be refreshable without intervention. Revoked access requires an explicit new decision. These states should not all become an endless retry loop.


Arcade’s custom-tool documentation explains declaring required authorization and injecting the authorized token into tool context. It also describes reinvoking the tool after the user completes a challenge. This is a useful lifecycle detail to exercise in a pilot.[Arcade tool authorization](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/build/create-tools/tool-basics/create-tool-auth) .


For each platform, test a user who has two accounts with the same provider. Ensure the intended connection is selected and remains visible in the execution evidence. Then test a revoked connection. The agent should receive an actionable explanation and a reconnection path, without silently switching to an unrelated account.


## Discovery quality affects productivity


Adding more tools to the model context can create ambiguity. Two actions might sound alike while one searches public data and another searches only the connected user’s workspace. A vague tool description can lead to correct syntax and the wrong task.


Build an evaluation set from actual user requests. Include a task with one obvious tool, a task with several plausible tools, a task requiring an account connection, and a task that should stop because the available tools cannot satisfy it.


Score selection, argument validity, and result usefulness independently. A platform may discover the right operation but require better parameter descriptions. Another may execute correctly while returning too much content for the agent to use efficiently.


Keep the model and request fixed when comparing platforms. If one trial receives hand-written hints and another receives only a generic request, the resulting difference says more about your test than the tool infrastructure. Our[schema-usability protocol](https://o11.ai/blog/test-agent-tool-schema-usability) gives a concrete way to isolate this variable.


## Execution history should answer real questions


When a user reports that the agent acted in the wrong account, operators need more than a timestamp and a green status. They need the intended user, selected connection, action, arguments, policy decision, outcome, and enough provider evidence to investigate.


Arcade documents execution history scoped to projects, with additional authority required to inspect sensitive inputs and outputs. That distinction matters: broad access to an activity list need not imply broad access to customer payloads.[Arcade tool execution history](https://docs.arcade.dev/en/operate/governance/tool-executions) .


Evaluate the same boundary in your own product. Decide which records support customer self-service, which require workspace administration, and which belong to an internal operator. A log that helps debugging can also contain private documents or personal information.


For funded work, add the funding source, reserved maximum, reported charge, and reconciliation state. A completed tool call and a settled charge are related events, but an application should not erase one because the other is delayed. Ask whether you can export sufficient evidence to reconcile a customer dispute without exposing provider secrets.


## Run a pilot that matches the product


Use a three-part pilot: read data from an authorized test account; enrich it with one paid public-data operation; and prepare an action for review. Keep the final action in draft form unless sending or writing is part of your explicitly approved test.


Define success before running it. For the account read, verify the tenant and required fields. For enrichment, verify identity matching and source evidence. For the proposed action, verify that it uses the correct destination and does not claim something unsupported by the research.


Then exercise one failure at each layer: missing permission, malformed tool arguments, and a timeout after submission. Record whether an ordinary user can recover, whether an administrator is needed, and whether repeating the request risks duplication.


Measure active setup time as well as total elapsed time. An OAuth review or supplier approval can add waiting time with little engineering effort; a confusing input contract can consume an afternoon. Both affect a launch, but they call for different remedies. The[time-to-first-call measurement guide](https://o11.ai/blog/measure-time-to-first-tool-call) separates these components.


## Choose by the work you need to remove


Composio belongs on a shortlist for agents operating across connected apps, including workflows that can use its supported Instant tools. Verify the exact actions and the spending enforcement your application needs.


Arcade belongs on a shortlist when user authorization, custom tools, and controlled execution are central to the product. Exercise the complete consent and reconnection flow, along with your requirements for buying additional services.


o11 belongs on a shortlist when a shared tool interface, explicit customer-versus-wallet account selection, and scoped paid execution fit your application. Confirm activation and live evidence for each required supplier before treating the implementation as launch-ready.


The best choice can include more than one layer. A business-data connection layer and a pay-per-use capability layer can coexist if identity, policy, and result ownership remain clear. Consolidate where it removes repeated engineering work; retain a direct integration where it gives your product necessary control.


Write down the responsibilities your application still owns after adopting the platform. The useful outcome is a smaller, clearer integration surface that lets developers ship productive agents, with an honest account of the work that remains.
